## "Something's wrong here" is not a bug report

A transcription can feel wrong while refusing to tell you where. Validation is
how you turn that broad unease into a short list of places to hear again. A
bar-length assertion finds missing time. A range check catches an improbable
register. A leap report flags intervals big enough to be worth comparing against
the source. None of them proves a pitch is correct. Each one deletes a family of
routine mistakes from your search.

Three rhythmic errors account for most of the damage: a missing tie, a rest
counted twice, and a dotted value entered as though it were plain. All three
change how much time is in a bar, so one exact total catches all three without
your having to guess which happened. Range and leap rules are softer, because
music breaks both on purpose all the time. Report those as evidence for a person
to review, never as edits the program is allowed to make on its own.

Once the structural checks go quiet, loop the suspicious bar next to the same
few seconds of the source. A short comparison lets you attend to attack time,
then pitch, then release, in separate hearings. Replay a whole minute and you
give yourself too many plausible culprits at once.

## A validator that stops, and one that only speaks up

```{.ruby audio=""}
use_bpm 80
use_synth :piano

bars = [
  [
    {note: 60, start: 0.0, duration: 1.0},
    {note: 62, start: 1.0, duration: 1.0},
    {note: 64, start: 2.0, duration: 2.0}
  ],
  [
    {note: 67, start: 0.0, duration: 1.0},
    {note: 79, start: 1.0, duration: 1.0}, # octave leap: review
    {note: 76, start: 2.0, duration: 2.0}
  ]
]

define :validate_bar do |events, expected_beats|
  total = events.map { |event| event[:duration] }.sum
  raise "bar totals #{total}, expected #{expected_beats}" unless total == expected_beats

  events.each_cons(2) do |left, right|
    leap = (right[:note] - left[:note]).abs
    puts "REVIEW leap of #{leap} semitones" if leap >= 12
  end
end

define :play_events do |events|
  events.each do |event|
    play event[:note], release: event[:duration] * 0.8
    sleep event[:duration]
  end
end

bars.each do |bar|
  validate_bar bar, 4.0
  play_events bar
end
```

Both bars account for four beats, so nothing halts. In bar 2 the jump from G4 to
G5 is impossible to miss, and the log reports its twelve-semitone size. So is
that octave a transcription error or the best thing in the melody? The program
has no opinion, and shouldn't. It found an observation and stopped there.

That distinction is the whole design. `raise` is for properties that cannot be
true of a correct transcription. `puts` is for properties that are usually worth
a second look.

## Break it three ways

1. Shorten the last duration in bar 1 from 2.0 to 1.5 and run the buffer. The
   assertion stops playback before the malformed measure can hide inside a
   longer listening pass. Read the reported total, put the half beat back, and
   watch bar 2 become reachable again.
2. Change note 79 to 80. The leap is thirteen semitones now and the line reaches
   A-flat5. Add a range warning for anything below 48 or above 84. You'll get two
   messages describing one event from different angles, and that's fine. Keep
   both if each points at a different question about the source.
3. Loop `play_events bars[1]` three times and compare it against the matching
   moment in your source. First time through, listen only to attacks. Second
   time, only pitches. Third, only releases. The bar holds still while your
   attention moves, which is the opposite of what happens when you replay the
   whole piece.

## What assertions can and can't know

An assertion encodes a property your representation must satisfy. In 4/4, an
ordinary complete bar accounts for four beats, counting rests and any part of a
tied continuation that occupies time. A pickup genuinely has a different
expected length, so give that measure its own value. Do not weaken every
assertion to tolerate the one exception, because that throws away the
information the test existed to protect.

Absolute event starts buy you more checks. Sort events by start, reject negative
durations, and find gaps or overlaps the source doesn't have. A sequential array
is faster to type, since each duration implies the next start, but an absolute
timeline is far easier to compare against a score or a recording, because one
bad duration doesn't shift every coordinate after it. Convert between the two
forms in a helper. Two hand-maintained versions will disagree, and you won't
find out when.

Warnings do a different job. A leap wider than an octave is ordinary in
arpeggiated music and may be the most characteristic thing about a line. A
plausible range depends on instrument, singer, octave convention and
transposition. Software shows you where an assumption was exceeded. The source
and the musical context decide whether the event should change, and neither of
those lives in your program.

There's a failure mode worth naming here, because it's the one that actually
bites. A check that fires constantly gets ignored, and an ignored check is worse
than no check, because it looks like coverage. If your leap warning prints on
every third note, the threshold is wrong for this music. Raise it, or scope it
to the bars you're unsure about. A validation report you skim is a validation
report that isn't running.

The milestone for this part is a thirty-to-sixty-second melody with a source
reference, bar-level data, validation helpers and a separate expressive
renderer. Ruby syntax checks confirm the program parses. Automated tests inspect
totals and ranges. Neither can confirm that your attacks match the recording or
that the shaped performance is convincing. Those stay manual Sonic Pi work, and
saying so is not a failure of the tooling; it's an accurate description of where
the tooling ends.

## Write the report, then read it honestly

Add a validation report to the transcription you built in [Lesson 45](45-transcribe-from-score.qmd). List every
bar total, the overall note range, all leaps of twelve semitones or more, and
each `REVIEW` marker.

Pick one suspicious bar and build a temporary three-stage loop: neutral rhythm,
strict pitches, then expressive rendering. Resolve each failure, or keep it and
write down the source-based reason it survives. A useful report can still be
full of warnings. What makes it useful is that you can say, for every surviving
one, why it's there.
